problem: The answer uses the bipartite balance test as if it proves the cycle exists: 'K₃,₃ has parts of size 3 and 3, so it has a Hamiltonian cycle.' Equal parts are only a necessary condition, never a guarantee, so the reasoning is invalid even though the conclusion for K₃,₃ is true.
fix: Answer: K₃,₃ does have a Hamiltonian cycle, for example a₁-b₁-a₂-b₂-a₃-b₃-a₁. The balance test alone cannot prove this; it only rules graphs out. K₃,₄ has parts 3 and 4, which are unequal, so by the balance test it has no Hamiltonian cycle.

problem: Euler path is first defined as a walk that 'is not closed', but the next paragraph says 'If zero vertices have odd degree, an Euler circuit exists and is also an Euler path.' The two statements contradict each other and a student may lose marks repeating the first one.
fix: Define one general term, Euler trail: a walk using every edge exactly once. If it is closed it is an Euler circuit; if it is open it is an Euler path. Then add: when no vertex has odd degree, the graph has a closed trail, which some books also count as an Euler path.

problem: 'A Hamiltonian cycle cannot contain a cut vertex' is wrong as written: C is a vertex of the graph, so any Hamiltonian cycle would contain C. The valid statement is about the graph, not the cycle.
fix: If a graph has a cut vertex, it has no Hamiltonian cycle: deleting C would leave two parts {A, B} and {D, E}, while deleting one vertex from a cycle always leaves a single connected path.
